Title:
Flipping Bits in Memory Without Accessing Them: An Experimental Study of DRAM Disturbance Errors

Research Fields:
Computer Architecture; Memory Systems; Cybersecurity

Keywords:
DRAM; disturbance errors; row hammer; memory reliability; memory security; PARA; probabilistic adjacent row activation

Research Problem:
The paper investigates DRAM disturbance errors, a phenomenon where repeatedly activating (opening/closing) the same DRAM row corrupts data stored in nearby rows, violating memory isolation. It aims to expose the widespread existence of these errors in commodity DRAM chips, characterize their behavior, identify their root cause, and propose a low-overhead solution to prevent them.

Methods:
FPGA-based testing platform with DDR3-800 memory controller; TestBulk and TestEach test procedures; User-level assembly program (Code 1a) inducing DRAM accesses; PARA (probabilistic adjacent row activation) mechanism; Binomial distribution error probability analysis; Cycle-accurate DRAM simulator for performance evaluation

Summary:
This paper exposes and characterizes DRAM disturbance errors (the "row hammer" phenomenon), where repeatedly activating the same DRAM row corrupts data in nearby rows, violating memory isolation. The authors demonstrate the phenomenon on real Intel (Sandy Bridge, Ivy Bridge, Haswell) and AMD (Piledriver) systems using a user-level program that continuously reads from DRAM, inducing thousands of bit-flips. They identify the root cause as repeated toggling of a row's wordline, which stresses inter-cell coupling effects that accelerate charge leakage from nearby rows. Using an FPGA-based testing platform, they characterize 129 DDR3 DRAM modules (972 chips) from three major manufacturers, finding disturbance errors in 110 modules (836 chips), with all modules manufactured in 2012-2013 being vulnerable. Key findings include: it takes as few as 139K activations to induce an error, up to one in 1.7K cells is susceptible, victim cells are predominantly localized to the two immediately adjacent rows, errors affect only charged cells (causing them to discharge), and errors are mostly repeatable but not strongly correlated with weak cells or temperature. The paper examines six potential solutions (better chips, ECC, frequent refreshes, cell retirement by manufacturer or end-user, and hot-row detection) and finds them all limited. It then proposes PARA (probabilistic adjacent row activation), a stateless low-overhead mechanism where each time a row is opened/closed, an adjacent row is refreshed with low probability p. PARA provides a strong statistical guarantee against disturbance errors (error probability as low as 9.4e-14 over one year with p=0.001 and Nth=100K) while incurring only 0.197% average performance degradation across 29 benchmarks.

Title:
Paxos Made Live - An Engineering Perspective

Research Fields:
Distributed Systems; Fault-Tolerance

Keywords:
Experiences; Fault-tolerance; Implementation; Paxos

Research Problem:
The paper addresses the practical challenges of moving the Paxos consensus algorithm from theory to a production-ready fault-tolerant database, including algorithmic gaps in the literature, software engineering challenges, and unexpected real-world failures.

Methods:
Paxos consensus algorithm; Multi-Paxos; Master leases; Epoch numbers; Group membership; Snapshots with snapshot handles; MultiOp database primitive; State machine specification language with compiler to C++; Runtime consistency checking with checksums; Randomized failure-injection testing (safety and liveness modes); Catch-up mechanism for lagging replicas; Batching of submitted values

Summary:
This paper describes the engineering experience of building a production fault-tolerant database at Google based on the Paxos consensus algorithm, used to replace the commercial third-party database (3DB) underlying the Chubby lock service. The authors detail the architecture, where a fault-tolerant replicated log based on Paxos sits at the bottom of the protocol stack, with a fault-tolerant replicated database on top, and Chubby using that database. They describe algorithmic challenges and solutions: handling disk corruption (via checksums, GFS markers, and non-voting rebuild), master leases to serve reads locally, epoch numbers to detect master turnover, group membership changes, snapshots with snapshot handles, and the MultiOp primitive providing atomic transaction-style support. They also discuss software engineering methods including a state machine specification language compiled to C++, runtime consistency checking via periodic checksums, and repeatable randomized failure-injection testing in safety and liveness modes. The paper documents unexpected production failures over 100+ machine years, including thread starvation causing master failover cascades, upgrade script failures causing data loss, semantic mismatches between database and Chubby, memory corruption, and OS bugs. Performance measurements show the Paxos-based system outperforms 3DB by 1.2x to 4.4x across various workloads. The authors conclude that significant gaps remain between Paxos theory and practice, and argue the fault-tolerance community should develop better tools and testing approaches, drawing a comparison to the compiler construction field.

Title:
Processing in Storage Class Memory

Research Fields:
Computer Architecture; Storage Systems

Keywords:
Processing-in-Memory; Storage Class Memory; Non-Volatile Memory; Data Processing Units; In-Storage Processing; Compression; Format Parsing

Research Problem:
The paper addresses the scalability problem in the storage subsystem, where CPU cycles and memory bandwidth become bottlenecks as storage performance increases. It proposes using Processing-in-Memory (PIM) processors integrated with Storage Class Memory (SCM) to offload simple data-processing tasks (e.g., compression, encryption, format conversion) from the host CPU to in-storage processors.

Methods:
Processing-in-Memory (PIM) architecture using UPMEM Data Processing Units (DPUs); Snappy decompression algorithm implemented on PIM hardware; SIMDJSON multi-line parsing benchmark; WiredTiger wtperf performance suite; DMA-based data copy benchmark for throughput measurement

Summary:
This position paper argues that Processing-in-Memory (PIM) will become an integral part of future Storage Class Memory (SCM) systems, enabling data processing to be performed in-storage to save memory bandwidth and CPU cycles. The authors identify typical data-processing tasks suited for in-storage processing, including compression, encryption, and format conversion. They describe the UPMEM PIM hardware architecture (Data Processing Units embedded in DRAM) as a proxy for future PIM on SCM, discussing design considerations such as inter-PIM communication, address translation, core density, and instruction set. They propose a wishlist for future PIM architectures including data triggered functions, concurrent memory access, mixing of memory types, and performance tuning. Feasibility experiments show that format parsing overhead is higher relative to total time on NVRAM (42%) than on HDD (13%), and that compression overhead is higher on NVRAM than HDD for 17 of 35 benchmark operations. A Snappy decompression implementation on PIM hardware achieved a speedup of nearly 4.5x with the largest file using 172 DPUs, and a throughput measurement showed approximately 252 GB/sec, more than 13x the theoretical bandwidth of a single DDR4-2400 channel. The paper concludes that PIM on SCM is a promising direction for offloading simple tasks to free CPU cycles and memory bus cycles.

Title:
B4: Experience with a Globally-Deployed Software Defined WAN

Research Fields:
Computer Networks; Software Engineering

Keywords:
Centralized Traffic Engineering; Wide-Area Networks; Software-Defined Networking; Routing; OpenFlow

Research Problem:
How to build a cost-effective, scalable private wide-area network connecting Google's data centers using Software Defined Networking principles, achieving high link utilization and efficient traffic engineering that traditional WAN architectures cannot provide.

Methods:
Software Defined Networking (SDN); OpenFlow; Centralized Traffic Engineering (TE); Max-min fair allocation; Tunnel Group Generation algorithm; Tunnel Group Quantization; ECMP hashing; Paxos leader election; Onix (modified) for OpenFlow Control; Quagga BGP/ISIS routing stack; Routing Application Proxy (RAP); IP-in-IP encapsulation; Linear Programming (LP) comparison baseline

Summary:
This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of B4, Google's private Software Defined WAN connecting its data centers worldwide. B4 was motivated by unique characteristics: massive bandwidth requirements across a modest number of sites, elastic traffic demand seeking to maximize average bandwidth, and full control over edge servers and network enabling rate limiting and demand measurement at the edge. These led to an SDN architecture using OpenFlow to control relatively simple switches built from merchant silicon. The architecture has three layers: switch hardware, site controllers (Network Control Servers hosting OpenFlow controllers and Network Control Applications), and a global layer with logically centralized applications (SDN Gateway and central TE server). B4 integrates existing routing protocols (BGP/ISIS via Quagga) with OpenFlow-based switch control through a Routing Application Proxy, enabling hybrid deployments and a gradual rollout. The centralized traffic engineering service allocates bandwidth among competing applications using max-min fair allocation, with bandwidth functions capturing relative application priority. The TE optimization algorithm (Tunnel Group Generation and Tunnel Group Quantization) achieves similar fairness and at least 99% of LP bandwidth utilization with 25x faster performance. TE drives links to near 100% utilization while splitting flows among multiple paths. B4 has been in production for three years, carries more traffic than Google's public facing WAN, and achieves 2-3x efficiency improvements over standard practice. The paper reports on deployment evolution, TE operations performance, failure impact, link utilization and hashing effectiveness, and lessons from a substantial outage. Key findings include near-100% link utilization, 14% average throughput improvement over shortest-path routing, hitless OFC/TE server failovers, and challenges in the OFC-OFA packet IO path and hardware programming overheads. The paper concludes that while the architecture does not generalize to all SDNs or WANs, the hybrid approach of supporting existing routing protocols alongside novel TE services demonstrates an effective technique for gradually introducing SDN into existing deployments.

Title:
Collection Tree Protocol

Research Fields:
Computer Networks; Wireless Sensor Networks; Routing Protocols

Keywords:
Collection; CTP; Sensor Network; Routing; Datapath Validation; Adaptive Beaconing; Trickle

Research Problem:
How to design a wireless sensor network collection routing protocol that remains efficient, robust, and reliable in the presence of highly dynamic link topologies, addressing the challenges of link dynamics and transient loops.

Methods:
Datapath validation; Adaptive beaconing (extension of the Trickle algorithm); Four-bit link estimator; Per-client queuing; Hybrid send queue; Transmit timer (rate-limiting to avoid self-interference); Transmit cache (duplicate suppression); ETX (expected transmissions) routing metric; Hysteresis in path selection

Summary:
This paper presents and evaluates two principles for wireless routing protocol design: datapath validation and adaptive beaconing, implemented in CTP Noe, an implementation of the Collection Tree Protocol (CTP) for wireless sensor networks. Datapath validation uses data packets to actively validate the routing topology and detect loops by having each data packet carry the transmitter's distance estimate, allowing detection of routing inconsistencies precisely when a route is needed. Adaptive beaconing extends the Trickle algorithm to routing control traffic, dynamically adapting the beacon interval between 64ms and one hour, resetting to the minimum on three events: forwarding a packet from a node with non-higher ETX, a significant cost decrease, or receiving a packet with the pull bit set. CTP Noe also includes data plane mechanisms: per-client queuing, a hybrid send queue, a transmit timer to avoid self-interference, and a transmit cache for duplicate suppression. The protocol is evaluated on 12 testbeds (20-310 nodes, seven platforms, six link layers) on both interference-free and interference-prone channels. Results show CTP Noe delivers over 90% of packets in all cases (many achieving 99.9%), sends 73% fewer beacons than MultihopLQI while reducing loop recovery latency by 99.8%, drops 90% fewer packets while sending 29% fewer packets, and achieves duty cycles of 3% while supporting aggregate loads of 30 packets/minute. The paper concludes that the efficacy of these techniques suggests wireless protocol limitations may be addressed by judiciously integrating data and control planes.

Title:
Remote Memory Calls

Research Fields:
Computer Networks; Computer Architecture

Keywords:
Remote Memory Calls; RDMA; SmartNIC; 1-sided RDMA; 2-sided RDMA; remote memory access

Research Problem:
The paper addresses the gap between the narrow set of 1-sided RDMA operations implemented in NIC hardware and the broader, more complex memory access patterns required by real distributed applications, which currently forces applications to either use inflexible 1-sided operations or CPU-expensive 2-sided operations.

Methods:
Remote Memory Calls (RMCs); RMCRegister operation; RMCInvoke operation; readhost() host memory access function; Modeling of latencies for linked list scan and remote buffer hashing workloads; Microbenchmark comparing RDMA read throughput between NIC-Host and Host-Host

Summary:
This paper proposes Remote Memory Calls (RMCs), an extension to RDMA that allows applications to install customized 1-sided RDMA operations. RMCs are memory-oriented software procedures registered and invoked by a client and executed by a remote server's RDMA NIC CPUs, supporting operations such as reading/writing host memory, atomics, conditional branching, monitoring writes, and basic computation. The paper argues that forthcoming CPU-based SmartNICs (focusing on Mellanox Bluefield-1) will have the hardware capabilities to efficiently support RMCs, and provides a feasibility analysis covering PCIe bandwidth, NIC-to-host memory access latency, and RMC execution rate. The authors identify host memory access latency, especially for small reads, as the main current impediment, but project that faster CPUs, new IO busses, and software improvements will resolve this. They model two workloads (linked list scanning and remote buffer hashing) comparing RMCs to 1-sided RDMA, finding that RMCs reduce network load and congestion but on current BF1 hardware do not reduce latency; however, idealized future SmartNICs would yield decreased latency for workloads with repeated host memory accesses. The paper also discusses implementation challenges including low-cost memory isolation, preemption and scheduling, and programming language design, and analyzes tradeoffs between RMCs, 1-sided, and 2-sided operations, arguing that RMCs as an abstraction enable runtime decisions about remote memory access location.

Title:
Deep Learning with Differential Privacy

Research Fields:
Machine Learning; Computer Vision; Cybersecurity

Keywords:
differential privacy; deep learning; neural networks; moments accountant; stochastic gradient descent; privacy accounting

Research Problem:
How to train deep neural networks with non-convex objectives under a modest ("single-digit") differential privacy budget, providing rigorous privacy guarantees for models trained on sensitive crowdsourced datasets, while keeping costs in software complexity, training efficiency, and model quality manageable.

Methods:
Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD); Moments accountant; Gradient norm clipping; Gaussian noise mechanism; Per-example gradient computation; Differentially private PCA; Numerical integration for privacy loss moments; Pre-trained convolutional layers; Mini-batch SGD

Summary:
This paper presents a framework for training deep neural networks with differential privacy guarantees. The authors develop a differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm that clips per-example gradient norms and adds Gaussian noise, combined with a new privacy accounting method called the moments accountant. The moments accountant tracks higher moments of the privacy loss random variable, providing tighter privacy bounds than the strong composition theorem—saving a sqrt(log(1/delta)) factor in epsilon and a Tq factor in delta. The approach is implemented in TensorFlow, including an efficient per-example gradient operator, a privacy accountant, and differentially private PCA. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that deep networks with non-convex objectives can be trained under modest ("single-digit") privacy budgets: on MNIST, 97% test accuracy is achieved with (8, 10^-5)-differential privacy, and on CIFAR-10, 73% accuracy with (8, 10^-5)-differential privacy. The paper also analyzes the effect of hyperparameters such as lot size, noise level, learning rate, clipping bound, PCA dimensions, and number of hidden units on accuracy under privacy constraints.

Title:
Defects4J: A Database of Existing Faults to Enable Controlled Testing Studies for Java Programs

Research Fields:
Software Engineering

Keywords:
Bug database; real bugs; testing framework

Research Problem:
Empirical studies in software testing research are often not comparable, reproducible, or characteristic of practice because real bugs are too infrequently used, with hand-seeded faults or mutants commonly used as substitutes. The paper addresses the challenge of extracting, reproducing, and isolating real bugs from version control history to enable reproducible testing studies.

Methods:
Automated identification of bug-fixing commits from version control and bug tracking systems; Automated reproduction of bugs by removing failing tests and executing test suites on faulty versions; Manual review and isolation of bug fixes from source code diffs; Database abstraction layer for version control and build systems; Test execution framework with components for test monitoring, test suite manipulation, test generation (EvoSuite), mutation analysis (Major), and code coverage analysis (Cobertura, CodeCover)

Summary:
This paper presents Defects4J, a database and extensible framework that provides real bugs to enable reproducible, controlled testing studies for Java programs. The initial version contains 357 real bugs from 5 large open source programs (JFreeChart, Closure Compiler, Commons Math, Joda-Time, Commons Lang). Each bug is accompanied by a comprehensive test suite with at least one test that exposes the bug (passes on the fixed version but fails on the faulty version). The paper describes a methodology for reproducing and isolating real bugs from version control history: automated identification of bug-fixing commits, automated reproduction by removing failing tests and executing suites on faulty versions, and manual review/isolation of bug fixes to exclude unrelated changes such as features or refactorings. Defects4J provides a database abstraction layer that abstracts heterogeneous version control and build systems, giving uniform access to faulty and fixed program versions and build targets. It also features a test execution framework with components for monitoring test execution, test suite manipulation, test generation (using EvoSuite), mutation analysis (using Major), and code coverage analysis (using Cobertura and CodeCover). The paper compares Defects4J to related work including SIR, iBugs, and the Siemens benchmark suite, highlighting advantages in number of real bugs, isolation of bugs, and the comprehensive test execution framework. Future work includes adding more programs and bugs and improving bug metadata with classification.

Title:
The Promises and Perils of Mining GitHub

Research Fields:
Software Engineering; Mining Software Repositories

Keywords:
Mining software repositories; git; GitHub; code reviews; bias

Research Problem:
What are the promises and perils of mining GitHub for software engineering research, specifically regarding the quality and properties of data available from GitHub and the biases that can affect research conclusions.

Methods:
Quantitative analysis of the GHTorrent dataset; Manual inspection of 434 GitHub repositories; Exploratory online survey of GitHub users (240 respondents); Small follow-up survey of 100 GitHub users (27 respondents); Heuristics for detecting pull requests merged outside GitHub (H1-H4)

Summary:
This empirical study investigates the promises and perils of mining GitHub data for software engineering research. The authors used a mixed-methods approach combining an exploratory survey of 240 GitHub users, quantitative analysis of the GHTorrent dataset, and manual inspection of 434 randomly selected repositories. They identified nine perils: (I) a repository is not necessarily a project (forks must be aggregated with base repositories); (II) most projects have very few commits (median of 6); (III) most projects are inactive (46% inactive in the last six months); (IV) a large portion of repositories are not for software development (only 63.4% of the manual sample); (V) two thirds of projects are personal (71.6% of repositories); (VI) only a fraction of projects use pull requests and their use is skewed; (VII) GitHub records only reworked commits, not original ones, when pull requests are updated; (VIII) most pull requests appear as non-merged even when actually merged (only 37% merged via GitHub facilities, with heuristics identifying an extra 42%); and (IX) many active projects do not conduct all development in GitHub (23% of committers are not GitHub users). The paper also highlights two promises: GitHub provides valuable data for studying code reviews via pull requests, and the interlinking of developers, pull requests, issues, and commits provides a comprehensive view of development activities. The authors developed heuristics (H1-H4) to detect pull requests merged outside GitHub and provide recommendations for researchers on how to select appropriate projects and avoid biases, such as considering projects with a balance of commits and pull requests and more than 2 committers/authors.

Title:
node2vec: Scalable Feature Learning for Networks

Research Fields:
Machine Learning; Recommender Systems; Natural Language Processing

Keywords:
Information networks; Feature learning; Node embeddings; Graph representations

Research Problem:
Learning continuous feature representations for nodes in networks that capture the diversity of connectivity patterns, balancing homophily and structural equivalence, in a scalable and task-independent manner.

Methods:
node2vec algorithm; 2nd order biased random walks; Skip-gram architecture extended to networks; Stochastic gradient descent (SGD); Negative sampling; Alias sampling; Binary operators for edge features (Average, Hadamard, Weighted-L1, Weighted-L2); One-vs-rest logistic regression classifier with L2 regularization; k-means clustering

Summary:
The paper proposes node2vec, an algorithmic framework for learning continuous feature representations for nodes in networks. node2vec learns a mapping of nodes to a low-dimensional feature space that maximizes the likelihood of preserving network neighborhoods of nodes. The key contribution is a flexible notion of a node's network neighborhood, achieved through a family of biased 2nd order random walks governed by two parameters: the return parameter p and the in-out parameter q. These parameters allow the search to smoothly interpolate between breadth-first sampling (BFS), which captures structural equivalence, and depth-first sampling (DFS), which captures homophily. The objective is optimized using stochastic gradient descent with negative sampling, extending the Skip-gram architecture to networks. The paper also extends node features to edge features using simple binary operators (Average, Hadamard, Weighted-L1, Weighted-L2). Experiments on multi-label classification (BlogCatalog, PPI, Wikipedia) and link prediction (Facebook, PPI, arXiv ASTRO-PH) show node2vec outperforms state-of-the-art methods (DeepWalk, LINE, Spectral Clustering) by up to 26.7% on classification and 12.6% on link prediction. The algorithm is semi-supervised, robust to noisy or missing edges, and scales linearly to networks with millions of nodes in a few hours. The Hadamard operator is found to be the most stable for link prediction.

Title:
Good r-Divisions Imply Optimal Amortized Decremental Biconnectivity

Research Fields:
Dynamic graph algorithms; Graph Theory

Keywords:
Dynamic graphs; 2-connectivity; graph minors; r-divisions; graph separators

Research Problem:
Whether decremental (deletion-only) connectivity, 2-edge connectivity, biconnectivity, or minimum cut for general graphs can be solved in amortized constant time per edge-deletion, or whether non-trivial lower bounds exist. The paper addresses maintaining biconnectivity, 2-edge connectivity, and connectivity under edge and vertex deletions for large classes of graphs including planar and minor-free graphs.

Methods:
r-divisions (strict (r,s)-divisions); nested r-divisions / suitable pair of r-divisions; BC-trees (block-cutpoint trees); compressed BC-forest; patchwork graph; bicapacitated biconnectivity; fully dynamic biconnectivity data structure; characteristic ancestor queries; first-on-path queries; union-find (weighted quick-find); look-up tables for polyloglog-size regions; recursive separator / sparsification techniques

Summary:
The paper presents a data structure for decremental (deletion-only) biconnectivity. Given a graph G with n vertices and m edges and a suitable pair of nested r-divisions, the structure preprocesses G in O(m+n) time and handles any series of edge-deletions in O(m) total time while answering pairwise biconnectivity queries in worst-case O(1) time. For non-biconnected vertex pairs, it can return the nearest cutvertex separating them in O(1) time. The approach generalizes and improves upon the planar decremental connectivity result of Lacki and Sankowski, extending from planar graphs to r-divisible graphs and from plain connectivity to 2-edge connectivity and biconnectivity. The key technical tools are the compressed BC-forest (obtained from block-cutpoint trees by contracting paths between critical nodes), the patchwork graph (stitching compressed BC-forests of regions together via shared boundary vertices), and bicapacitated biconnectivity (viewing the BC-forest as a bicapacitated graph where non-bridge blocks have capacity 2). The structure uses nested r-divisions with three levels (top, middle, bottom), where bottom-level regions of polyloglog size are handled via look-up tables to achieve O(1) update and query time in the practical RAM model. Decremental changes are modeled by three operations: path deletions, block splits, and pseudoblock contractions, which are handled by a fully dynamic biconnectivity data structure. Nearest cutvertex queries are answered via characteristic ancestor queries on dynamic trees. As a consequence, the paper obtains optimal amortized decremental biconnectivity, 2-edge connectivity, and connectivity for planar, bounded genus, and minor-free graphs, with a linear-time algorithm for computing r-divisions in minor-free graphs. The question of whether the data structure generally admits vertex deletions in O(n) total time remains open.

Title:
3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering

Research Fields:
Computer Vision; Computer Graphics; Machine Learning

Keywords:
novel view synthesis; radiance fields; 3D gaussians; real-time rendering; anisotropic splatting; tile-based rasterization

Research Problem:
Achieving high-quality novel-view synthesis with real-time rendering at 1080p resolution and competitive training times, which previous radiance field methods could not simultaneously provide for unbounded and complete scenes.

Methods:
3D Gaussian scene representation; Anisotropic covariance optimization; Interleaved optimization with adaptive density control (clone and split densification); Spherical harmonics for view-dependent color; Tile-based differentiable rasterizer with GPU radix sort; Alpha-blending of anisotropic splats with visibility ordering; Stochastic gradient descent optimization with L1 and D-SSIM loss

Summary:
This paper introduces 3D Gaussian Splatting, a method for real-time radiance field rendering that achieves state-of-the-art visual quality with competitive training times. The method represents scenes using a set of 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, each defined by position, opacity, anisotropic covariance, and spherical harmonic coefficients. Three key components are introduced: (1) 3D Gaussians as a flexible, explicit, differentiable volumetric scene representation that avoids computation in empty space; (2) interleaved optimization and adaptive density control (clone and split operations) that optimizes anisotropic covariance for accurate scene representation; and (3) a fast, visibility-aware, tile-based differentiable rasterizer using GPU radix sort that supports anisotropic splatting with alpha-blending and allows an unlimited number of splats to receive gradients. The method is evaluated on the Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending, and synthetic Blender datasets. Results show quality on par with or slightly better than Mip-NeRF360 (the previous quality state-of-the-art) while achieving real-time rendering at 93-135 fps and training times of 35-45 minutes (compared to 48 hours for Mip-NeRF360). Ablations demonstrate the importance of SfM initialization, clone/split densification, anisotropic covariance, spherical harmonics, and unlimited gradient depth complexity. The authors note limitations including artifacts in poorly observed regions, popping artifacts, and higher memory consumption than NeRF-based solutions.

Title:
Conformer: Convolution-augmented Transformer for Speech Recognition

Research Fields:
Automatic Speech Recognition; Machine Learning; Natural Language Processing

Keywords:
speech recognition; attention; convolutional neural networks; transformer; end-to-end

Research Problem:
How to combine convolution neural networks and transformers to model both local and global dependencies of an audio sequence in a parameter-efficient way for automatic speech recognition.

Methods:
Conformer block (feed-forward, multi-headed self-attention, convolution, and second feed-forward modules in a Macaron-style sandwich structure); Multi-headed self-attention with relative sinusoidal positional encoding (Transformer-XL); Convolution module with pointwise convolution, gated linear unit (GLU), 1-D depthwise convolution, batchnorm, and swish activation; Macaron-style half-step feed-forward modules; Convolution subsampling module; SpecAugment data augmentation; Variational noise regularization; Adam optimizer with transformer learning rate schedule; 3-layer LSTM language model with shallow fusion

Summary:
The paper introduces Conformer, a convolution-augmented Transformer architecture for end-to-end automatic speech recognition. The Conformer block consists of four stacked modules: a feed-forward module, a multi-headed self-attention module, a convolution module, and a second feed-forward module, arranged in a Macaron-style sandwich structure with half-step residual connections. The self-attention module uses relative sinusoidal positional encoding from Transformer-XL, while the convolution module uses a pointwise convolution with GLU gating, a 1-D depthwise convolution, batchnorm, and swish activation. The authors evaluate three model sizes (Conformer S/M/L with 10M, 30M, and 118M parameters) on the LibriSpeech benchmark. The large model achieves state-of-the-art WER of 2.1%/4.3% without a language model and 1.9%/3.9% with an external language model on test/testother. The medium model outperforms the previously published Transformer Transducer which uses 139M parameters. Extensive ablation studies examine the effects of the convolution block, Macaron-style feed-forward modules, relative positional embeddings, swish activation, attention head count, convolution kernel sizes, and different strategies for combining convolution and self-attention modules. The authors conclude that the convolution module is the most critical component, and that placing it after the self-attention module works best for speech recognition.

Title:
Flipping Bits in Memory Without Accessing Them: An Experimental Study of DRAM Disturbance Errors

Research Fields:
Computer Architecture; Memory Systems; Cybersecurity

Keywords:
DRAM; disturbance errors; row hammer; memory reliability; memory security; PARA; probabilistic adjacent row activation

Research Problem:
The paper investigates DRAM disturbance errors, a phenomenon where repeatedly activating (opening/closing) the same DRAM row corrupts data stored in nearby rows, violating memory isolation. It aims to expose the widespread existence of these errors in commodity DRAM chips, characterize their behavior, identify their root cause, and propose a low-overhead solution to prevent them.

Methods:
FPGA-based testing platform with DDR3-800 memory controller; TestBulk and TestEach test procedures; User-level assembly program (Code 1a) inducing DRAM accesses; PARA (probabilistic adjacent row activation) mechanism; Binomial distribution error probability analysis; Cycle-accurate DRAM simulator for performance evaluation; Memtest86+ environment; Statistical analysis of data patterns

Summary:
This paper exposes and characterizes DRAM disturbance errors (the "row hammer" phenomenon), where repeatedly activating the same DRAM row corrupts data in nearby rows, violating memory isolation. The authors demonstrate the phenomenon on real Intel (Sandy Bridge, Ivy Bridge, Haswell) and AMD (Piledriver) systems using a user-level program that continuously reads from DRAM, inducing thousands of bit-flips. They identify the root cause as repeated toggling of a row's wordline, which stresses inter-cell coupling effects that accelerate charge leakage from nearby rows. Using an FPGA-based testing platform, they characterize 129 DDR3 DRAM modules (972 chips) from three major manufacturers, finding disturbance errors in 110 modules (836 chips), with all modules manufactured in 2012-2013 being vulnerable. Key findings include that as few as 139K activations can induce an error, up to one in 1.7K cells is disturbable, victim cells are predominantly localized to two adjacent rows of the aggressor row, and errors are mostly repeatable and weakly influenced by temperature. The paper examines seven potential solutions and proposes PARA (probabilistic adjacent row activation), a stateless low-overhead mechanism that refreshes adjacent rows with a small probability each time a row is opened and closed. PARA provides a strong statistical guarantee against disturbance errors (error probability of 9.4e-14 over one year with p=0.001 and Nth=100K) while incurring only 0.197% average performance degradation across 29 benchmarks.

Title:
GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation

Research Fields:
Natural Language Processing; Machine Learning

Keywords:
GloVe; word representation; word vectors; global log-bilinear regression; co-occurrence matrix; word analogy

Research Problem:
The paper addresses the question of how meaning is generated from corpus co-occurrence statistics and how word vectors can represent that meaning, specifically aiming to construct a model that captures linear directions of meaning (as probed by word analogy tasks) while efficiently leveraging global corpus statistics.

Methods:
GloVe (Global Vectors) model; Weighted least squares regression; Global log-bilinear regression; AdaGrad optimization; Stochastic sampling of nonzero co-occurrence elements; Conditional random field (CRF) for NER; Singular value decomposition (SVD) baselines; word2vec (skip-gram and CBOW) comparison models

Summary:
The paper introduces GloVe (Global Vectors), a new global log-bilinear regression model for learning word vector representations. The authors analyze the model properties needed for linear semantic and syntactic regularities to emerge in word vectors, arguing that ratios of co-occurrence probabilities are the appropriate starting point. They derive a weighted least squares objective that trains only on the nonzero elements of a word-word co-occurrence matrix, combining the advantages of global matrix factorization methods (like LSA) and local context window methods (like skip-gram). The model uses a weighting function f(x) with parameters xmax=100 and alpha=3/4, trained with AdaGrad. The paper shows the relationship between GloVe and skip-gram/ivLBL models, and provides a complexity analysis showing the model scales as O(|C|^0.8) under a power-law assumption. Experiments on the word analogy task (75% accuracy on a 42B token corpus), five word similarity tasks, and the CoNLL-2003 NER benchmark show GloVe outperforms other models including word2vec, SVD baselines, HPCA, HSMN, and CW. The paper also analyzes the effects of vector length, context window size/type, corpus size, and training time on performance.

Title:
Deep Kernel Learning

Research Fields:
Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Kernel Methods

Keywords:
deep kernel learning; Gaussian processes; spectral mixture kernels; KISS-GP; kernel interpolation; Kronecker algebra; Toeplitz algebra; inducing points

Research Problem:
How to combine the structural properties of deep learning architectures with the non-parametric flexibility of kernel methods to create scalable, expressive covariance kernels for Gaussian processes, overcoming the Euclidean/absolute distance limitations of standard kernels and the O(n^3) scaling of standard GPs.

Methods:
Deep kernel learning (DKL); Spectral mixture (SM) base kernels; RBF base kernels; KISS-GP approximation with local cubic kernel interpolation; Inducing points on a regular multidimensional lattice; Kronecker and Toeplitz structure exploiting algebra; Linear conjugate gradients (LCG) for inference; Backpropagation through the Gaussian process marginal likelihood; Deep feedforward fully-connected networks; Convolutional neural networks; Caffe-based DNN implementation

Summary:
The paper introduces scalable deep kernels that combine the structural properties of deep learning architectures with the non-parametric flexibility of kernel methods. The authors transform the inputs of a base kernel (RBF or spectral mixture) with a deep feedforward or convolutional architecture, then use local kernel interpolation, inducing points, and Kronecker/Toeplitz structure exploiting algebra (via the KISS-GP approximation) to create scalable closed-form covariance kernels for Gaussian processes. All deep kernel hyperparameters (network weights and base kernel parameters) are learned jointly by backpropagating derivatives through the Gaussian process marginal likelihood, without approximate Bayesian inference. The resulting model effectively has a hidden layer with an infinite number of adaptive basis functions, achieving O(n) training cost and O(1) per-test-point prediction cost. Experiments on a wide range of UCI regression datasets (including a 2-million-example dataset), Olivetti face orientation extraction, MNIST digit magnitude extraction, and step function recovery show that DKL consistently outperforms scalable Gaussian processes with expressive kernels, stand-alone deep neural networks, and GPs applied to the outputs of trained deep networks. The spectral mixture base kernel provides notable additional performance gains over RBF, and the learned kernels reveal interpretable structure (e.g., faces with similar rotation angles become highly correlated). The approach also naturally produces posterior predictive distributions, useful for applications such as reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization.

Title:
Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction

Research Fields:
Human-Computer Interaction; Artificial Intelligence

Keywords:
Human-AI interaction; AI-infused systems; design guidelines

Research Problem:
The paper addresses the lack of unified, validated design guidelines for human-AI interaction, given that AI-infused systems can violate established usability guidelines due to their probabilistic, inconsistent, and unpredictable behaviors.

Methods:
Affinity diagramming; Modified heuristic evaluation; User study with heuristic evaluation; Expert evaluation; Maximum-variance sampling strategy

Summary:
This CHI 2019 paper proposes and validates 18 generally applicable design guidelines for human-AI interaction. The authors synthesized over 150 AI-related design recommendations from academic and industry sources into a set of guidelines organized into four temporal categories: "Initially" (G1-G2), "During interaction" (G3-G6), "When wrong" (G7-G11), and "Over time" (G12-G18). The guidelines were developed and refined through a four-phase process: (1) consolidating guidelines from industry products, public articles, and scholarly papers via affinity diagramming; (2) an internal modified heuristic evaluation that reduced the set from 20 to 18 guidelines; (3) a user study with 49 HCI practitioners who tested the guidelines against 20 popular AI-infused products across 10 categories; and (4) an expert evaluation of the revisions with 11 experts. The user study found 785 examples of the guidelines (313 applications, 277 violations, 89 neutrals, 106 "does not apply"), demonstrating broad relevance across product categories. Key findings include that explanation-related guidelines (G11) had high violation counts, guidelines on social norms and biases (G5, G6) were least clear and most often rated "does not apply," and voice assistants had the most "does not apply" instances. The authors discuss trade-offs between generality and specialization, note limitations for non-GUI systems and high-risk domains, and highlight the need for diverse evaluators to recognize social norms and biases.

Title:
Slide Rule: Making Mobile Touch Screens Accessible to Blind People Using Multi-Touch Interaction Techniques

Research Fields:
Human-Computer Interaction; Accessibility

Keywords:
Accessibility; blindness; mobile devices; touch screens; multi-touch interaction techniques; speech output

Research Problem:
Touch screens are largely inaccessible to blind users because interaction techniques require users to visually locate objects on the screen. The paper addresses this by developing audio-based multi-touch interaction techniques that enable blind users to access touch screen applications.

Methods:
One-finger scan gesture; Second-finger tap selection gesture; Multi-directional flick gesture; L-select gesture; Double-tap gesture; Lift-then-tap gesture; Slip timer for second-finger tap; User-centered design process with formative interviews and iterative prototyping

Summary:
The paper introduces Slide Rule, a set of audio-based multi-touch interaction techniques that make touch screen mobile devices accessible to blind users. Slide Rule provides a completely non-visual interface that repurposes a touch screen as a talking touch-sensitive surface, requiring only a standard multi-touch screen and audio output with no additional hardware. It uses four basic gesture interactions: a one-finger scan to browse lists, a second-finger tap to select items, a multi-directional flick for additional actions, and an L-select gesture for browsing hierarchical information, plus a double-tap gesture. The design was informed by formative interviews with 8 blind mobile device users and iterative prototyping with 3 blind users, guided by design principles including risk-free exploration, finger-resolution operation, reduced selection accuracy demands, quick browsing, intuitive gestural mappings, and the ability to query location and return home. The techniques were implemented in three prototype applications (Phone, Mail, Music) on an Apple iPhone. A user study with 10 blind participants compared Slide Rule against a button-based Pocket PC running Mobile Speak Pocket. Results showed Slide Rule was significantly faster (11.69s vs 12.79s mean task time), with significantly lower listening time per item, and was preferred by 7 of 10 participants. However, users made more errors with Slide Rule (0.20 errors per trial vs none for the Pocket PC), reflecting a speed-accuracy tradeoff. Questionnaire results showed the Pocket PC was rated significantly higher on ease of use, feeling in control, ease of learning, and familiarity, yet participants still preferred Slide Rule. The paper discusses design implications, the cost of errors, and future work including composite interaction techniques, text entry methods, support for larger displays, and applicability to sighted users in eyes-free contexts.

Title:
LINE: Large-scale Information Network Embedding

Research Fields:
Machine Learning; Natural Language Processing; Social Network Analysis

Keywords:
information network embedding; scalability; feature learning; dimension reduction

Research Problem:
The problem of embedding very large information networks (with millions of nodes and billions of edges) into low-dimensional vector spaces while preserving both local (first-order) and global (second-order) network structures, in a way that scales to real-world networks.

Methods:
LINE model with first-order proximity objective; LINE model with second-order proximity objective; Negative sampling; Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (ASGD); Edge-sampling algorithm using alias table method; Concatenation of first-order and second-order embeddings; Neighborhood expansion via second-order neighbors

Summary:
The paper proposes LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding), a network embedding model that maps vertices of very large information networks into low-dimensional vector spaces. LINE defines and preserves two complementary notions of proximity: first-order proximity (local pairwise proximity captured by observed edge weights) and second-order proximity (similarity of neighborhood structures, capturing shared neighbors). The model uses carefully designed objective functions for each proximity, optimized via negative sampling and asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. A key contribution is an edge-sampling algorithm using an alias table that samples edges proportional to their weights and treats them as binary edges, addressing the gradient explosion problem caused by high variance in edge weights. The overall time complexity is O(dK|E|), linear in the number of edges. The paper also discusses handling low-degree vertices (via adding second-order neighbors) and new vertices. Experiments on language (Wikipedia), social (Flickr, Youtube), and citation (DBLP) networks evaluate word analogy, document classification, and multi-label node classification. Results show LINE(2nd) outperforms baselines including graph factorization, DeepWalk, and SkipGram on word analogy; LINE(1st+2nd) significantly outperforms all methods on classification tasks; and LINE is efficient, processing networks with millions of nodes and billions of edges in a few hours on a single machine. The paper also analyzes performance with respect to network sparsity, parameter sensitivity, and scalability with multiple threads.

Title:
Trajectory-based Social Circle Inference

Research Fields:
Machine Learning; Information Retrieval; Recommender Systems

Keywords:
trajectory mining; variational auto-encoder; social circle inference

Research Problem:
Inferring users' social circles (friendships) based solely on their motion trajectories, without any explicit social network information, formulated as a multi-label classification problem. The problem faces challenges of data sparsity, varying sociability, and difficulty in feature exploitation.

Methods:
DeepTSCI framework; Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM); Autoencoder; Variational Autoencoder (VAE); Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) check-in embedding; Hierarchical softmax; Multi-label classifier (Friend Decoder); Dropout (variational inference based); KL cost annealing; Reparameterization trick

Summary:
The paper addresses Trajectory-based Social Circle Inference (TSCI), the problem of inferring users' social circles (friendships) based purely on their motion trajectories without any explicit social network information. The authors formulate TSCI as a multi-label classification problem and propose DeepTSCI, an RNN-based framework with three variants: DeepTSCI-LSTM/Bi-DeepTSCI (using LSTM and bidirectional LSTM), DeepTSCI-AE (using autoencoder pre-training), and DeepTSCI-VAE (using variational autoencoder). The framework embeds check-ins into low-dimensional vectors via CBOW with hierarchical softmax, splits trajectories into sub-trajectories, and uses a Friend Decoder multi-label classifier to predict friendship sets. Two subtasks are studied: RT-TSCI (predicting friends for existing users) and RU-TSCI (predicting friends for new users). Experiments on Brightkite, Gowalla, and Foursquare (Tokyo and New York) datasets show that DeepTSCI-VAE achieves the best performance across macro-R, macro-F1, and accuracy compared to baselines including Co-Visit, MF, Decision Trees, SVM, RandomForest, MLP, TULER, and DeepMIML. The authors note that RU-TSCI performance is relatively low due to a cold-start-like problem. Future work includes incorporating semantic inter-relationships among friends and reinforcement learning methods.
